business_model.claim: Costamare Inc. is an international owner and operator of containerships that charters its vessels primarily under long-term, fixed-rate time charters to leading liner companies for worldwide transportation of containerized cargoes.
quotes: We are an international owner and operator of containerships.
We charter our containerships to some of the world’s largest liner companies, providing worldwide transportation of containerized cargoes.

Our strategy is to deploy our containerships on long-term, fixed-rate time charters to take advantage of the stable cash flows and high utilization rates typically associated with long-term time charters.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in P1 and P3.
business_model.claim: Under time charter contracts, the charterer pays a fixed or index-linked daily hire rate (recognized on a straight-line basis) and covers most voyage expenses such as fuel and port charges, while the company pays vessel operating expenses.
quotes: Under our time charters the charterer pays for most voyage expenses, which generally include, among other things, fuel costs, port and canal charges, pilotages, towages, agencies, commissions, extra war risks insurance and any other expenses related to the cargoes, and we pay for vessel operating expenses, which generally include, among other costs, costs for crewing, provisions, stores, lubricants, insurance, maintenance and repairs, dry-docking and intermediate and special surveys.

Under a time charter agreement, the charterer pays a fixed charter hire rate or an index-linked charter hire rate (which is adjusted periodically based on a specific index such as the Baltic Exchange Handysize Index (“BHSI”)) for the use of the vessel.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in P1 and P5 (Notes 1 and 5).
business_model.claim: Through its controlled subsidiary Neptune Maritime Leasing Limited (NML)—in which it holds 75% of ordinary voting rights and raised its investment commitment to $247.8 million in January 2026—the company earns leaseback income by acquiring and bareboat chartering out 52 funded or committed shipping assets under sale and leaseback contracts with seller-lessee purchase obligations.
quotes: Under the NML segment, NML acquires and bareboat charters out the acquired vessels to the respective seller-lessees of the vessels, who have the obligation to purchase the vessel at the end of the bareboat agreement and the right to purchase the vessel prior to the end of the bareboat agreement at a pre-agreed price.

As of February 24, 2026, Neptune is currently funding or committed to funding 52 shipping assets, and Neptune’s portfolio of sale and leaseback arrangements and commitments includes 22 dry bulk vessels, three tanker vessels, 24 offshore vessels and three container vessels.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in P1 and P3.
business_model.claim: Containership voyage revenue is driven by fleet size, daily charter hire rates, and operating days/fleet utilization—which was 99.0% in 2023, 99.8% in 2024, and 99.6% in 2025—while contracted day coverage of 98.2% in 2026, 86.6% in 2027, and 71.6% in 2028 mitigates near-term rate cyclicality.
quotes: Our voyage revenues are driven primarily by the number of vessels in our fleet, the amount of daily charter hire that our vessels earn under time charter agreements and the number of operating days during which our vessels generate revenues.
In 2023, 2024 and 2025 our fleet utilization for each year was 99.0%, 99.8% and 99.6%, respectively.
Vessels operated under long-term charters are less susceptible to cyclical containership charter rates than vessels operated on shorter-term charters, such as spot charters.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in P2 (Item 3.D) and P3 (Item 5).
business_model.claim: Market charter rates respond to global container trade volumes, vessel rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope away from the Suez Canal (which helped raise average time charter rates by 163% in 2024 and 13% in 2025), trade protectionism or tariffs, and fleet capacity supply, with the global orderbook reaching 33.9% of existing capacity as of December 2025.
quotes: During 2024, containership charter rates increased by 163% on average.

This increase in charter rates was attributable to a 4.5% increase in the volume of containers transported due to increased demand and an increase of 4.7% in TEU-miles mainly due to container vessels still having to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope.

Furthermore, according to Clarksons Research, future supply as represented by the containership orderbook as of December 2025 amounted to 33.9% of the existing fleet capacity, higher than the respective percentage of 27.0% a year ago, representing the highest such percentages since 2011.

In addition, a substantial portion of our vessel operating expenses, primarily crew wages, are in currencies other than the U.S. dollar (mainly in Euro), and any gain or loss we incur as a result of the U.S. dollar fluctuating in value against these currencies is included in vessel operating expenses.

competitive_position.claim: A major competitive threat is potential capacity oversupply, as the global containership orderbook reached 33.9% of existing fleet capacity (up from 27.0% a year earlier), with 65.5% of that orderbook in vessels exceeding 12,000 TEU.
quotes: Furthermore, according to Clarksons Research, future supply as represented by the containership orderbook as of December 2025 amounted to 33.9% of the existing fleet capacity, higher than the respective percentage of 27.0% a year ago, representing the highest such percentages since 2011.

According to Clarksons Research, as of December 2025, the containership orderbook represented 33.9% of the existing fleet capacity, 65.5% of which was for vessels with carrying capacity in excess of 12,000 TEU.

An oversupply of large newbuild vessels and/or re-chartered containership capacity entering the market, combined with any decline in the demand for containerships, may reduce available charter rates and may decrease our ability to charter our containerships when we are seeking new or replacement charters other than for unprofitable or reduced rates, or we may not be able to charter them at all.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the cited items (20-F Item 3.D and Item 5).
competitive_position.claim: Regional armed conflicts and potential normalization of Suez Canal transits threaten supply-demand dynamics that previously elevated charter rates.
quotes: Following ceasefire discussions in October 2025, some liner companies have announced a possible return to the Suez route.
If such return materializes, it could distort the current supply and demand dynamics.

This increase in charter rates was attributable to a 4.5% increase in the volume of containers transported due to increased demand and an increase of 4.7% in TEU-miles mainly due to container vessels still having to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the cited item (20-F Item 3.D).
competitive_position.claim: Trade protectionism, tariffs, and proposed U.S. port fees on internationally built or Chinese-linked vessels threaten global container shipping demand and operating economics.
quotes: On November 10, 2025, U.S. and Chinese authorities suspended the application of each respective set of port fees for one year.
Substantial uncertainty remains as to how the port fees will be assessed after the end of the suspension period on November 10, 2026.

Notably, the MAP proposes a “universal infrastructure or security fee,” which would apply more broadly than the USTR special port fees and would cover all internationally built vessels calling at U.S. ports.

competitive_position.basis: Stated in the cited items (20-F Item 3.D and Item 5).
competitive_position.claim: Rising vessel maintenance and dry-docking demands—with 20 containerships scheduled for dry-docking in 2026 and 8 in 2027—alongside volatile vessel market values threaten cash flows and credit-facility compliance.
quotes: We have dry-docked 38 containerships over the past three years, and we plan to dry-dock 20 in 2026 and 8 vessels in 2027.
We expect that insurance costs, dry-docking and maintenance costs will increase as our vessels age.
In addition, any such deterioration in the market values of our vessels could trigger a breach of certain covenants under our credit facilities, which could adversely affect our operations.

If financing becomes unavailable when needed, or is available only on unfavorable terms, we may be unable to meet our future obligations as they come due.
